name: OyeChats
headline: Better answers start before the answer.
summary: Grounded conversations, more dependable retrieval, and a shorter path from question to useful answer.
role: Retrieval, prompt architecture, streaming & background jobs
context: OyeChats is a conversational product that answers from a website’s content, qualifies leads, and supports human handoff. A useful conversation depends on the retrieval and execution paths underneath it.
problem: Useful knowledge-base content was being excluded by a relevance gate. Duplicated retrieval paths and oversized assembled prompts also made the behavior harder to reason about.
changes: Retrieval diagnosis
I traced the relevance gate that excluded useful content, following the path from retrieved material to the answer rather than treating every refusal as a prompt problem.
A simpler execution path
I consolidated duplicated RAG pipelines and prompt assembly, and worked on streaming and durable qualification jobs so the conversation and its follow-up work could be handled more deliberately.
Evaluation-driven corrections
Later changes addressed regressions found in question evaluations, including company-context answers and long whitespace runs that could block a worker.
result_note: One assembled prompt, as documented in the remediation pull request. This is a prompt-size comparison, not a latency or answer-quality benchmark.
lesson: Retrieval gates, prompt assembly, and background execution all shape the answer a person sees. Diagnose that whole path before adding another instruction.

name: AlsoNotify
headline: Trust is a product feature.
summary: Authentication, safer email rendering, and reports that agree on what the numbers mean.
role: Frontend security, reporting consistency & email rendering
context: AlsoNotify brings task tracking, calendars, leave management, finance, reporting, and notifications into a shared work platform. Its frontend uses Next.js, React, and feature-based components.
problem: The same KPI could receive a different rating in the interface and the exported PDF. Protected page shells were guarded only in the client, while email styles were being dropped before their scoping code could run.
changes: One meaning for a number
I unified KPI thresholds so the employee drawer and PDF report use the same banding function. Previously, 72% occupancy could read Low on screen and appear green in the export.
A safer entry into the workspace
I constrained post-login redirects to local paths, added a server-side cookie-presence route guard, and tightened replay masking. Backend verification remains the authentication boundary.
Email styling with boundaries
I fixed the sanitizer path that discarded leading style blocks and corrected the scoping expression that broke media rules. Existing CSS sanitization then applies to those blocks as intended.
result_note: The documented reconciliation included 813 passing tests across 73 files. That is the verification reported for that change, not a current coverage claim for the entire product.
lesson: Consistency matters at the seams: an export should mean the same thing as the screen, and rendering a document should preserve its layout without allowing it to restyle the surrounding app.

name: CleanStart
headline: Fast for readers. Clear for editors.
summary: CMS performance, correct cache timing, and product interfaces that make the next step clearer.
role: CMS performance, caching, navigation & content journeys
context: CleanStart’s web and CMS experience connects security products, a content catalog, resources, and reader journeys. The same system has to work for someone publishing content and someone discovering it.
problem: Relationship lookups multiplied in the CMS list view, and cache invalidation could run before a database write committed. Publishing could leave a new resource unavailable until a later revalidation.
changes: Batch the repeated work
I batched CMS relationship lookups and separated publishing from integration work, reducing the request fan-out in the documented list view.
Make the timing correct
I moved cache purging after the write commits so revalidation reads the newly published state.
Design the next useful step
I worked on the reading-depth resource journey and its editor overrides, reduced the animation cost in a follow-up, and gave the Tricorder platform a clearer place in product navigation.
result_note: The documented 25-row CMS list view. This measures relationship requests for that example, not total page requests or a universal speedup.
lesson: Performance and correctness often meet at the same boundary. A fast invalidation at the wrong moment still gives the reader the wrong page.

name: VICTUS
headline: An assistant with tools. And boundaries.
summary: Document-aware orchestration with tool policies, approval controls, and inspectable execution traces.
context: VICTUS explores an assistant that can work with documents and call tools. The current backend and frontend repositories are the clearest entry points; the original project records an earlier iteration.
problem: An agent that can take action needs more than a fluent response. A person needs to understand what context was used, which actions are allowed, and what actually happened.
changes: Context before action
I built around document retrieval and AI orchestration so tool calls have a context path rather than appearing as isolated model output.
Policies in the execution path
Tool policies and approval controls make permissions part of the system. Behavior depends on the configured execution mode.
A trace people can inspect
Execution traces expose the path between request and action. The interface is part of making that path understandable.
result_note: An architectural focus, not a production performance claim. Inspect the current backend for the configured policy and approval behavior.
lesson: Inspectability belongs in the product. It is much easier to reason about an agent when its actions have explicit boundaries and a visible record.

name: INNEED
headline: Own less. Do more.
summary: A rental marketplace that follows the journey beyond a listing, through payment, return, and resolution.
context: INNEED is a rental marketplace connecting discovery with vendor onboarding, checkout, the rental lifecycle, disputes, and administration.
problem: Listings are only one part of a marketplace. Vendors and renters need the product to manage what happens after an order, including payment verification and exceptions.
changes: The complete lifecycle
I brought account and vendor workflows, listings, rental state, and administration into the same product.
Payments that connect to the order
The payment integration includes Razorpay and verification, with the rental workflow continuing beyond the checkout screen.
A place for exceptions
Disputes and administrative workflows give non-happy-path cases a place in the system.
result_note: The repository documents the implementation and setup. No adoption or transaction-volume claim is implied.
lesson: Designing a marketplace means following an order until it is resolved, not stopping when the payment button works.

name: Fynix
headline: The quote, the charge, the invoice. In agreement.
summary: Checkout edge cases, referral controls, tax-aware invoicing, and recovery workflows.
context: The Fynix work includes an event-registration and payment journey with country-based pricing, referral codes, invoicing, and administrative recovery.
problem: A large referral discount could create an order below the payment provider’s minimum. A currency-related payment decline also exposed internal error wording that gave the buyer no useful next step.
changes: Keep one price through the flow

I capped the discount percentage before the order was created so the quote, stored order, and rebuilt invoice continue to agree. The documented USD example changed a 99% discount to an effective 98% discount.
Explain an actionable retry
I replaced an opaque payment-failure message with a conditional country-and-currency hint, keyed to the order currency. The message does not pretend to know where the card was issued.
Operational tools
My work also covered tax-aware invoicing, referral limits, registration tooling, and manual recovery paths.
result_note: In the documented checkout case, the adjusted discount produced a $1.98 charge above the provider minimum. This is an example from that fix, not pricing guidance.
lesson: Payment UX depends on the data model. Keeping one stored discount driving the quote and invoice prevents a friendly interface from promising the wrong amount.

name: GKR Hospitality
headline: A lighter site. A stronger foundation.
summary: Image delivery, search visibility, contact-form protection, and considered maintenance.
context: GKR Hospitality is a public-facing website with a gallery, service information, reviews, and a contact journey. Its quality depends as much on delivery and discoverability as on appearance.
problem: Oversized imagery made delivery unnecessarily heavy. An inherited canonical pointed multiple pages at the homepage, and the contact and security foundations needed attention.
changes: Make imagery practical to deliver
I re-encoded 70 images, removed unused assets, and stopped serving gallery originals in the documented maintenance work.
Give each page its own identity
I corrected the sitewide canonical collapse, added sitemap and robots support, and improved page metadata and structured data.
Maintain the working site
I added server-side form validation, spam checking, and a Content Security Policy, and worked on fonts, navigation, and error states.
result_note: Combined weight of the 70 re-encoded image assets in the maintenance report. This is an asset-total comparison, not the bytes transferred on one page or a measured load-time improvement.
lesson: A polished website is an ongoing system: the images need to arrive, the right pages need to be discoverable, and the contact flow needs to work.

name: Multimodal Search
headline: Two ways to ask. One search space.
summary: Find an image with a sentence or another image, using a shared embedding space.
context: This application connects a text-or-image query to image retrieval with CLIP embeddings, ChromaDB, a FastAPI backend, and a React interface.
problem: Keyword search depends on labels. An image collection becomes more flexible to explore when a query can describe its meaning or simply be another image.
changes: Shared representation
I used CLIP to represent text and images in a shared embedding space.
An end-to-end retrieval path
ChromaDB handles vector retrieval and FastAPI exposes the search flow.
A usable model
The React interface connects the query to returned results so the model can be explored as an application.
result_note: An application workflow. No retrieval-accuracy or production-scale benchmark is claimed.
lesson: The model becomes useful through the whole query-to-result experience, including the interface that lets someone understand what it found.

name: Bitling
headline: A little company for the working day.
summary: A desktop companion that gives commits, tests, and deploys a little character.
context: Bitling is a desktop companion built primarily for macOS. It reacts to commits, test runs, deploys, and Claude Code sessions. A browser demo makes the character easy to try.
problem: Developer tools are usually all output and status. I wanted to explore a small, expressive interaction around the events already happening during a working day.
changes: Events become behavior
The companion connects developer activity to small moments of character.
Motion that feels coherent
I worked on pose transitions and character-specific behavior so the reactions feel connected.
A low-friction introduction
The browser demo lets a visitor try the playful side of the project without installing the desktop application.
result_note: The main desktop implementation targets macOS. The repository also records an unverified Windows port; it is not presented here as a tested release.
lesson: Playful interactions deserve the same attention to transitions, responsiveness, and clear feedback as any other interface.

name: GitHub Mirror
headline: A footprint with a visual signature.
summary: An alternative view of GitHub activity through deterministic visual signatures.
context: GitHub Mirror explores a GitHub footprint through repository and activity data, turning those inputs into deterministic visual signatures.
problem: A profile contains many traces of a person’s work. A different visual representation can make that footprint interesting to explore beyond a conventional repository list.
changes: A different representation
I explored visual signatures built from repository and activity data.
Deterministic mapping
The signature follows its inputs rather than being a random decoration.
Curiosity as a use case
The project sits between a developer tool and a visual experiment.
result_note: A creative exploration, not a score of developer ability or contribution quality.
lesson: A visualization is most interesting when its appearance has a clear relationship to the data behind it.

name: The World
headline: A GitHub history you can walk through.
summary: A playable 3D world derived from repository and commit history, with language districts and people behind the work.
context: The World, also called NULL, translates a GitHub history into an explorable place. Repository structures, language districts, and collaborators connect the scene to the record behind it.
problem: A long activity history is difficult to understand through a flat repository list. A spatial experience also needs navigation, readable interactions, and a useful alternative for visitors who cannot run WebGL.
changes: Let the record shape the scene
Repository structures derive their scale from commit counts and lifespan. Language districts use GitHub language colors and follow the chronology of the underlying history.
Make exploration useful
Movement, a world map, and nearby interaction prompts let visitors discover repositories, case studies, and collaborators. Touch controls support a different way to navigate.
Keep another path open
A text fallback presents the work when WebGL is unavailable. The portfolio uses recorded gameplay for its lightweight preview and starts the full game only when requested.
result_note: A creative representation of the repository’s recorded dataset. It is not a live count of current GitHub activity or a measure of developer ability.
lesson: An unusual interface works best when its shapes have a reason and visitors still have a direct, accessible route to the content.
